title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Explain the mechanical functions of a compression ring.
gradingNotes: Require sealing and sustained outward cylinder-wall contact.
commonMistakes: Describing only the piston groove or treating the ring as a rigid seal.
student: State the primary mechanical functions of a compression piston ring and explain why outward contact with the cylinder wall is required.
instructor: The compression ring helps seal combustion gases, transfers heat toward the cylinder wall, and controls the interface with the bore. Elastic outward contact is required to support sealing while the split ring accommodates installation and service motion.

title: External Actions and Constraints
learningObjectives: Identify the closing action and bore reaction.
gradingNotes: Require installation closing action and distributed bore contact reaction.
commonMistakes: Modeling the bore as a conventional beam support.
student: Identify the physical action that compresses the ring during installation and the distributed reaction supplied by the cylinder wall after installation.
instructor: Installation tooling and the cylinder entry close the split ring. In the installed condition, the bore geometrically restrains the ring and supplies distributed inward normal reactions while the ring acts outward on the wall.

title: Installed Boundary Condition
gradingNotes: Require a nominal circular geometric constraint, not a pin or fixed support.
student: Explain how the nominal cylinder bore acts as a geometric constraint on the split ring rather than as a conventional pin or fixed support.
instructor: The bore constrains the installed ring to a nominally circular boundary and reacts continuously through contact. It does not restrain one discrete point like a pin or clamp.

title: Closure Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace the closing action into wall contact.
gradingNotes: Require gap action, elastic ring body, and cylinder-wall contact.
commonMistakes: Stopping the path at the ring ends.
student: Trace the load path from the installation/closing action at the ring gap through the elastic ring and into the cylinder-wall contact reaction.
instructor: The tangential gap-closing action deforms the split ring; internal force and bending effects develop through the curved ring body, and the installed ring transfers outward normal contact action to the cylinder wall.

title: Critical Features
learningObjectives: Identify features governing closure and contact.
gradingNotes: Require the elastic ring body and end-gap region.
student: Identify the ring body and gap region as the primary features governing the closure/contact response.
instructor: The curved elastic ring body provides the closure stiffness and outward recovery action. The end-gap geometry records the change from free to installed state and is where the specified tangential closing force is defined.

title: Relevant Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Distinguish a mean-pressure model from local contact analysis.
gradingNotes: Require elastic closure and mean/equivalent pressure, with local distribution excluded.
commonMistakes: Claiming the calculated pressure is uniform everywhere.
student: Identify the mechanical responses evaluated here and explain why a detailed local contact-pressure distribution is beyond the simplified model.
instructor: The model evaluates free-to-installed elastic closure, section properties, mean/equivalent wall pressure, and equivalent normal force. A real local distribution requires curved-ring free-shape and contact analysis with geometry, bore distortion, gas loading, temperature, friction, wear, coatings, groove interaction, and possible twist.

title: Relevant Parameters
learningObjectives: Explain the role of each assigned variable.
gradingNotes: Expect d, m, s, a, h, E, and F_t with correct physical meanings.
commonMistakes: Using E to derive F_t in this simplified problem.
student: Identify the roles of d, m, s, a, h, E, and Ft in the physical behavior and simplified analysis.
instructor: d sets installed ring size; m and s define closure; a and h define the rectangular section; E characterizes the cast-iron elastic response; and specified Ft represents the tangential force associated with holding the ring at the installed gap. In this baseline, E provides material context but Ft is not derived from gap closure.

title: Student-Generated Ring Idealization
learningObjectives: Create free and installed split-ring models.
gradingNotes: Require both states, d, m, s, a, h, F_t, and distributed outward contact action.
commonMistakes: Replacing the curved ring with a straight cantilever or copying an instructor figure.
student:
Draw the piston ring in (a) its free state and (b) its installed state inside a nominal circular cylinder bore. Label d, m, s, axial width h, radial wall thickness a, tangential closing action Ft, and distributed outward contact action.

Student model / diagram space:
instructor: A suitable model shows a free split ring with gap m, and a nominally circular installed ring of diameter d with gap s. Opposed tangential closing forces act at the gap ends, the cylinder supplies distributed contact reaction, and the ring has a rectangular a by h section.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions bounding the mean-pressure model.
gradingNotes: Require the specified single-ring, elastic, circular, quasi-static, and mean-pressure assumptions plus exclusions.
commonMistakes: Using straight-beam closure or calling pressure locally uniform.
student: State the assumptions used to idealize the installed ring and mean/equivalent contact pressure.
instructor: Use a single-piece ring, linear-elastic behavior, small elastic strain, a nominally circular installed condition, a representative rectangular section, quasi-static installation, and a mean/equivalent wall-pressure model. Neglect gas pressure, friction, thermal effects, piston-groove contact, ring twist, wear, coatings, and local circumferential pressure variation. Treat Ft as specified; do not infer it from m − s using a straight-beam formula.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Organize the closure and pressure calculations.
gradingNotes: Require closure, section properties, force interpretation, pressure, contact area, force check, and limitations.
commonMistakes: Attempting to solve for F_t from E and gap closure.
student: Outline the calculation sequence needed to quantify ring closure, section properties, mean wall pressure, and equivalent normal contact force.
instructor: Calculate Δg = m − s, then A and I; interpret the specified Ft; calculate pm = 2Ft/(hd); calculate nominal area πdh; evaluate Neq = pmπdh; and verify it equals 2πFt.

title: Free-to-Installed Gap Closure
learningObjectives: Calculate the reduction in end gap.
gradingNotes: Require Δ_g = m − s with millimeter units.
commonMistakes: Adding the gaps or reporting a negative closure.
student: Determine the required reduction in ring end gap, Δg = m − s, during installation.

title: Ring Cross-Section Properties
learningObjectives: Calculate rectangular section area and in-plane inertia.
gradingNotes: Require A = ah and I = ha^3/12 with correct units and stiffness interpretation.
commonMistakes: Interchanging a and h in the cubic term.
student: For the rectangular ring section, determine A = ah and the in-plane bending second moment of area I = ha3/12. Explain why radial wall thickness strongly affects bending stiffness.
instructor: A = ah = ({{piston_a_mm}})({{piston_h_mm}}) = {{piston_area_mm2}} mm2. For in-plane ring bending, I = ha3/12 = {{piston_I_mm4}} mm4. The cubic dependence on a makes radial wall thickness especially influential on bending stiffness.

title: Tangential Closing Force
gradingNotes: Require a force associated with maintaining the installed gap, not a straight-beam derivation.
commonMistakes: Attempting to compute F_t from E(m-s) with an axial or cantilever formula.
student: State what the specified tangential closing force Ft physically represents and why it is associated with maintaining the ring at its closed-gap condition.
instructor: The specified Ft = {{piston_F_t_N}} N is the opposed tangential force applied at the ring ends for the installed/closed-gap condition. It is a piston-ring parameter associated with the elastic recovery action that produces wall contact. Real closure is a curved-member/contact response, so this baseline does not derive Ft from gap closure using a straight-member formula.

title: Mean Cylinder-Wall Contact Pressure
commonMistakes: Omitting the factor of two or using cross-sectional area ah.

title: Equivalent Total Normal Contact Force
learningObjectives: Relate mean pressure to equivalent total normal force.
gradingNotes: Require A_contact = πdh, N_eq = p_mA_contact, and check 2πF_t.
commonMistakes: Using the ring cross-sectional area rather than nominal cylindrical contact area.
student: Calculate the nominal cylindrical contact area and equivalent total normal contact force. Show that the result is also 2πFt.
instructor: Acontact = πdh = {{piston_contact_area_mm2}} mm2. Then Neq = pmAcontact = {{piston_normal_force_N}} N. Independently, 2πFt = {{piston_normal_force_check_N}} N, confirming the same result.

title: Engineering Assessment
learningObjectives: Interpret mean pressure without overstating the model.
gradingNotes: Require mean-versus-local distinction, at least three excluded effects, and free-shape control.
commonMistakes: Calling p_m the exact uniform local pressure.
student: Explain whether the calculated pressure is the exact local pressure everywhere. Identify at least three excluded real effects and explain why piston-ring manufacturing must control the free shape, not only nominal diameter.
